Analysis · Quantz · Flute Concerto in G Major, QV 5:174 · Movement III

III. Presto

The finale, quick and light, in 2/4. Five ritornellos and four solos, and every ritornello is built from the same three blocks of the first: the head and its rise to D, a pedal with a forte answer, and a tonic pedal with closing cadences. Below: the form, every cadence, and the partimento patterns, on a playable score.

  • 278 bars, 2/4
  • 5 ritornellos, 4 solos
  • Keys G → D → E minor → G
  • 38 cadences marked
  • 84 pattern brackets

Form at a Glance

Ritornellos (blue) and solos (amber), the key areas, and below them where each instrument plays: the solo flute, the strings of the tutti, and the basso continuo. Click a section to find it on the score.

Ritornello (tutti)SoloFlute (solo)StringsBasso continuo

The ritornellos shrink and change: R2 is blocks A and B in D, R3 only block B in E minor, R4 only the head, and R5 blocks B and C, so the movement ends as the first tutti did. The basso drops out under most solo passages, and a violin or the viola takes the bass (bassetto). Section boundaries and keys are our reading ours.

Cadences

Every cadence marked on the score, with the evidence from the bass and the figures. All labels are our reading ours.

  • One closing formula. 4 with ⁶₅, 5, 1 (as C, D, G) ends block B and block C of every ritornello and most solos: mm. 26, 36, 38, 89, 114, 159, 169, 238, 256, 266, 276, 278.
  • Six-four cadences are rare: only the cadence in D that closes the main part of Solo 1 (mm. 74–75) and the held D of mm. 234–236 before the last solo cadence.
  • Half closes mark each move to a new key: D (m. 12, again in mm. 100 and 221), A as V of D (m. 57), B as V of E minor (mm. 136, 173), and D before the last climb (m. 185).
  • Elision: the next section starts on the cadence note at mm. 89, 114, 159, 207 and 256: the soloist’s last note is the tutti’s first, or the other way round.
  • Quantz’s breaks: the cadences of mm. 4 and 8 are the main breaks on the fourth and eighth bars that he asks for (XVIII §39).
  • Keys reached by cadence: D major (mm. 55, 58, 75, 87, 89, 104, 110, 114), E minor (mm. 152, 159, 165, 169), and G (all the rest).

Partimento Patterns

The bass patterns under the movement, named with partimento and galant terms (the rule of the octave, Gjerdingen’s schemata). Each reading rests on the bass line and Quantz’s figures; the names are modern labels, not Quantz’s guideline. The buttons scroll to the place and play it.

Schema

Prinner

Bass 4–3–2–1 with sixths on 3 and 2, under 6–5–4–3: C–B–A–G under E–D–C–B (mm. 6–8). The tutti uses it to interrupt the flute (mm. 44–46, 215–217), and R2 has it in D (mm. 94–96).

Bass figure

Rise to the Dominant

G–A–B–C♯–D: the bass climbs from the tonic to the dominant with the raised fourth (mm. 10–12, 48–50, 219–221), and a fifth higher in R2 (mm. 98–100). Each time a pedal on the new dominant follows.

Texture

Pedal and Forte Answer

The violins repeat the dominant, piano, while the melody turns around one note; the basso enters forte and a scale runs down to the cadence (mm. 13–15, 17–19). The pair returns under the flute (mm. 51–52, 118–119, 125–126, 226–227).

Schema

Romanesca

A bass that falls a fourth and rises a step: D–A–B–F♯–G (mm. 62–67) and G–D–E–B–C–G (mm. 191–196), both in the viola, under broken chords in the flute falling by step.

Schema

Monte

A climb by step, each step reached through its own dominant: B–C, C♯–D, D♯–E in Violin II, the lowest part while the basso rests (mm. 127–132). It moves the music from G to E minor in six bars. There is no Fonte (the falling counterpart, minor then major a step lower) anywhere in this movement.

Schema

Ponte

A held dominant that bridges to a return: B in Violin II under the flute’s climb, which leads back to E minor (mm. 173–178), and the same on D, which leads to G (mm. 185–190).

Cadence

Converging Cadence

The bass rises 4–♯4–5 to a half close while the melody falls to 2: it ends each Prinner block before the cadence (mm. 23–24, 56–57, 111–112, 166–167, 263–264).

Cadence

Cadenza Semplice and Composta

The plain cadence (bass 4–5–1, the 5 on one beat) closes nearly every block; the composta holds 5 for a whole bar with ⁶₄–⁵₃ above it, here only at mm. 73–74 and 234–236.

Sequence

Circle of Fifths

E, A⁷, D⁷, G⁷, C⁷, F♯⁷, B⁷, E (mm. 145–152), one root a bar under the flute’s broken chords: the last stretch of Solo 2 before the cadence in E minor.

Performing the Flute Part

The blue marks above the flute staff apply Quantz’s rules on breathing, tonguing and dynamics to this movement ours; the red marks above them are the printed marks of the Suzuki Flute School edition revised by Toshio Takahashi, for comparison. Hover any mark for its source. Both layers can be switched off above the score.

Rules We Apply Quantz

Paraphrased from the Versuch, chapters VI (tonguing), VII (breathing), XI and XII (the Allegro), Reilly pp. 71–135.

  • Breath ’: take it from a long note, never from a short one or the last note of a bar (p. 87); before a new idea (p. 88); in running sixteenths after the first note of a group, which is shortened; a wide leap is the best place (p. 89). Strokes and rests give the breath for free.
  • ti and di: eighths that leap take ti, the short firm stroke; eighths that move by step take the softer di (p. 73). Where the fastest notes are sixteenths, the eighths stay short and the quarters sing (XII §22, p. 133, written for the Allegro assai, which is in the Presto’s tempo class). So the falling scale of the head is short but soft.
  • ti‿ti ri ti: when sixteenths are too quick for diri, slur the first two notes and tongue the third with ri and the fourth with ti; Quantz recommends this above the other ways (p. 78).
  • did’ll: the double tongue, for the quickest passage-work only (pp. 79–80). At ♩ = 160 the sixteenths here are eight to a pulse beat, the limit Quantz sets (p. 284).
  • Echo: a repeated figure changes dynamic, Piano after Forte (p. 133). Swell: long notes grow and fade (p. 132). Accent: dissonant appoggiaturas louder than their resolution (pp. 254–255), and the low note of a deep leap stronger (p. 132).
  • Inequality: in very fast passage-work only the first of every four sixteenths is held a little; nothing under dots, strokes or repeated notes (pp. 123–124).

Takahashi’s Edition comparison

Printed marks only (pages 10–12 of the flute part); the handwritten notes in the copy are left out. Breitkopf, the source of our score, prints almost nothing in the solos beyond slurs on a few figures, strokes on cadence notes and dots on the head’s falling eighths.

They agree on most breaths and on the echoes in mm. 60, 141 and 205. They differ on the stroke of the head’s falling eighths (hard dots against a soft di), and most on the grouping of slurs in the sixteenth passages, and the pedal bars, where Takahashi builds to forte and Quantz’s rule gives an echo.

The Articulation View

Choose Articulation above the score for three flute staves over the bass: Fl., the part as Breitkopf prints it; Fl. Q., our Quantz reading engraved as notation ours; and Fl. T., Takahashi’s printed marks. Only Fl. Q. sounds at first; turn on Fl. or Fl. T. to hear the others.

  • Fl. Q.: a staccato dot on each unslurred eighth and a tenuto line on each quarter where the Allegro rule applies (eighths short, quarters sung: XII §22, p. 133); a slur over the first two of each four sixteenths where we read ti‿ti ri ti (VI, p. 78); did’ll and di passages left without slurs, since the tongue does the work; a comma for each breath; an accent on the appoggiaturas (pp. 254–255). Breitkopf’s own slurs, dots and strokes stay.
  • Fl. T.: Takahashi’s slurs, dots, accents and breath marks, his wedges for Breitkopf’s strokes, the notes he ties over Breitkopf’s rests (mm. 173–190), the appoggiatura of mm. 55–56 written out, and the 8va passages written at the pitch he gives.
  • The clearest contrast is in the sixteenths: Quantz slurs two and tongues two (mm. 58–67), Takahashi tongues one and slurs three, or slurs whole bars (mm. 129–140).

Quantz’s Rules and This Movement

Rules Quantz

Paraphrased from Versuch XVIII §§38–39, the last Allegro of a concerto (Reilly pp. 314–315), with XVII.vii on tempo.

  • The last Allegro differs from the first in its ideas and its meter, and is jocular and gay (§38, p. 314). If the first is in common time and the Adagio in triple, 2/4 is one of the choices. Here: 4/4, 3/4, 2/4.
  • The three movements should not begin on the same note: one on the keynote, another on the third, the third on the fifth (§38, p. 315). Here: movement I starts on G, movement II on B♭, and this movement on D.
  • Same key as the first movement, but the keys should come in a different order (§38, p. 315). Here the order is the same as in movement I: G, D, G, E minor, G. Quantz’s own concerto does not follow his rule on this point.
  • The ritornello is short, gay, fiery and playful; the solo melody is pleasing, fleeting and light (§39, rules 1 and 2). The ritornello here is 38 bars, about 28 seconds at the tempo below.
  • Easy passage-work that differs from the first movement’s (rule 3). Here the solo passages are mostly broken chords (mm. 58–66, 137–151, 191–196) and lines that climb over a pedal (mm. 173–178, 185–190); compare them with movement I.
  • Strict meter: the first caesura at the start of the second bar, the main breaks on the fourth and eighth bars (rule 4). Here the held D of m. 1 gives way on the downbeat of m. 2, and mm. 4 and 8 close on G.
  • The accompaniment is not too full (rule 5). Here the basso drops out for whole passages and the viola or Violin II carries the bass with repeated notes.
  • Tempo. Presto belongs to Quantz’s first class, with Allegro assai (XVII.vii §49, p. 284); in 2/4 a quick Allegro takes one pulse beat a bar (§51, p. 286). With the pulse at 80, a half note is 80 and a quarter 160, the page’s default.

Guidelines and Our Readings guideline ours

  • Pattern names. Prinner, Romanesca, Monte, Ponte and the converging cadence are Gjerdingen’s names for galant schemata; the rule of the octave is a partimento term. We apply them from the bass line and the printed figures.
  • Cadence types (PAC, IAC, HC) are modern labels. We call a cadence perfect only when the bass goes 5–1 in root position and the melody ends on 1.
  • Three blocks. We divide R1 into A (mm. 1–15), B (mm. 16–26) and C (mm. 26–38) because the later ritornellos take them whole: R2 is A and B in D, R3 is B in E minor, R4 is the head of A, R5 is B and C.
  • Bass in the upper strings. Both Romanescas (mm. 62–67, 191–196) are in the viola, and the Monte (mm. 127–132) and both Pontes (mm. 173–178, 185–190) in Violin II, while the basso rests: the bass patterns that carry the solos are in the bassetto, not the continuo.
  • The same key order as movement I. The finale keeps the plan of the first movement (D, then E minor) against §38; the difference lies in the proportions: here the E-minor part is longer and reached by a Monte.

Notes on the Reading

The Score

The score follows the Breitkopf edition: five staves (flute, Violin I, Violin II, viola in the alto clef, basso with its figures), with the beams, slurs, strokes, staccato dots, trills, appoggiaturas, dynamics and rehearsal letters as printed. Where two violins share a staff in the edition, they are written as two layers.

Flute + Basso Continuo keeps only the outer staves. In the solos this is how the movement sounds with a keyboard realizing the figures; where the basso rests (the bassetto passages), the bass line of the full score lies in the strings and is missing from this view.

Source and Check

Transcribed from the Breitkopf & Härtel score edited by Horst Augsbach (scan supplied by the user), 278 bars. Each part was read from the scan and checked bar by bar against full-size crops of every system, with staff lines measured where a pitch was in doubt.

Playback: a baroque ensemble at A = 415 by default (flute, violins, viola, cello with harpsichord, each from its own recorded samples), a harpsichord alone at A = 415, or the Steinway Grand at A = 440. Slurred notes are joined, strokes and dots shortened. Trills start on the upper note; appoggiaturas take half the main note (two thirds of a dotted note), following Quantz VIII (Reilly p. 95). The movement has no cadenza: Quantz reserves cadenzas for slow pieces and serious quick ones (XV §4, p. 180), and this finale is neither.
